extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Locke's criteria and conceptual distinctions for relations, cause and effect, and identity (personal, animal, vegetable, substances). Useful for analyzing philosophical arguments about what grounds relations and personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any idea may be the foundation of relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Any idea, whether simple or complex, may be the occasion why the mind brings two things together and so forms a relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: naming Caius 'husband' brings to mind the contract and ceremony of marriage; calling him 'whiter' brings to mind the colour white. Any idea that occasions such comparison can ground a relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relations with correlative terms are obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terms that have correlative counterparts (e.g., father/son, husband/wife, bigger/less) are obvious and immediately perceived as relational because the correlatives reciprocally intimate one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where languages provide correlatives, people readily perceive the relation; absence of a correlative term can make a relation less obvious (e.g., concubine without a correlative).

rubrics_metrics.name: External denominations where language lacks correlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Names that include relations but lack a correlative in a language are often treated as 'external denominations' and their relational character is less readily noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that words still signify some idea; if it refers to something distinct from the thing named, it includes a relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seemingly absolute terms can conceal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some terms that appear absolute (OLD, GREAT, IMPERFECT, etc.) tacitly contain relations to other things or standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke promises to expand on this in later chapters; these terms may imply comparison even when they seem to signify intrinsic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation is distinct from the things related
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of relation consists in referring or comparing two things one to another; relations are extrinsic to the things compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'father' is a notion superinduced to the substance 'man' and refers only to an act relating him to a child.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of relation can occur without change in the things related
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation (and its consequent denomination) can cease or change without any alteration in one of the relata; relations depend on the presence or absence of the correlative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Caius ceases to be a father by the death of his son though he himself is unaltered; comparing the same person to different others can yield contrary denominations (older/younger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation requires two things
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no relation except between two things considered as two; the whole considered as one (e.g., a triangle) is a positive idea, but relations arise only from comparison of distinct items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relation always involves two ideas or things, and a ground or occasion for their comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: All things are capable of almost infinite relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing (simple idea, substance, mode, or relation) can be considered in reference to an almost infinite number of other things, producing numerous relations and denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example list: a single man may be father, brother, son, friend, enemy, European, Englishman, possessor, captain, superior, inferior, bigger, less, older, younger, contemporary, like, unlike, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of relations can be clearer than ideas of the related subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative ideas (e.g., paternity, friendship) are often clearer and more distinct in our minds than the complex ideas of the substances to which they attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the notion of 'paternity' can be easier to form than the general idea of 'humanity'; knowing a single action can give a clear idea of a relation even if the substance remains obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations terminate in simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Though relations can be numerous and remote from sense, they ultimately terminate in simple ideas derived from sensation or reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke intends to show how comprehensive relations (e.g., cause/effect) are built from simple ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words that lead the mind beyond the subject are relative
rubrics_metrics.description: Any word that necessarily leads the mind to ideas other than those supposed to exist in the thing signified is a relative word (e.g., father, brother, king, blacker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute words (man, black, merry) signify only what is supposed to exist in the thing named; relative words imply something exterior as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: All relatives are made up of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of relations, however refined, are ultimately composed of simple ideas of sensation or reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke will illustrate this by treating the relation of cause and effect and other major relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of cause and effect arise from observing constant sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: From observing that particular qualities and substances begin to exist and receive their existence from the application of other beings, we form the ideas of cause and effect: the cause is that which produces an idea, the effect is that which is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heat producing fluidity in wax (heat as cause, fluidity as effect); fire producing ashes from wood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: That which produces any simple or complex idea is denoted by 'cause'; that which is produced is denoted by 'effect'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To have the idea of cause and effect it suffices to consider any simple idea or substance as beginning to exist by the operation of some other, without knowing the manner of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among creation, generation, making, and alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke distinguishes kinds of originating relations: CREATION (thing wholly new, no part existed before), GENERATION (a thing constituted from pre-existing particles but not existing as that whole), MAKING (extrinsic cause producing by sensible composition), ALTERATION (a new simple idea produced in a subject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a new particle of matter (creation); a man or egg produced from pre-existing particles (generation); an artificial object (making); a change in a subject's quality (alteration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and place as foundations of relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations of time and place form extensive relations; words answering HOW LONG or WHEN reflect relations of duration or temporal distance to a measuring period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Queen Elizabeth 'lived sixty-nine' indicates relation of duration measured by solar years; dating events (1066) shows distance from a chosen epoch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of age and magnitude are relative to species-specific standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'young' and 'old' or 'great' and 'little' are relative: they compare an instance to the standard idea of ordinary duration or size for that kind of thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man is 'old' at 70, a horse at 20, a dog at 7; a 'great horse' differs by cultural/ breed standards (Welsh vs. Flemish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations of place and extension are comparative
rubrics_metrics.description: Denominations about place and distance (above, below, a mile from X) are relations; size and bulk (great/little) are likewise comparative to settled ideas of species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural/observational standards determine what counts as 'great' or 'little'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute terms often function as relative denominations
rubrics_metrics.description: Words thought absolute (weak/strong, necessary/stores) often express relations by comparison to some standard or intended end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'weak' denotes lack compared to usual power; 'necessary stores' relates to completing the intended voyage or future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity consists in sameness of something at determinate time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity is formed by considering anything as existing at a determined time and place and comparing it to itself at another time; identity holds when the ideas attributed do not vary from the earlier moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that two things of the same kind cannot exist in the same place at the same time; identity follows from having one beginning of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of substances: God, finite intelligences, bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: We have ideas of three sorts of substances: God (eternal, unalterable, everywhere), finite spirits (each has determinate time/place of beginning), and bodies (particles of matter whose identity persists absent addition/subtraction of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each sort has its own grounds for identity: e.g., God has no identity problem; finite spirits and particles of matter are individuated by their particular beginning in time/place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of modes and relations determined like substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes and relations, terminating in substances, have their identity and diversity determined through the same considerations, though successive existences (motions, thoughts) differ because they have different temporal beginnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions and thoughts, being successive, cannot be the same at different times because each perishes on beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principium individuationis: existence determines individuation
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of individuation is existence itself — a being's particular time and place of existence determine its identity and distinguish it from other beings of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke illustrates with an atom and masses of atoms; the continuity or change of parts can affect whether a mass remains the same body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of vegetables: persistence of the same life/organization
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant is the same plant so long as it partakes of the same continued life and organization, even if particles of matter change; identity depends on the organization that conveys the common life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An oak remains the same oak while it partakes of the same life and continued organization, despite gradual material turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of animals: organized life and internal motion
rubrics_metrics.description: An animal's identity resembles a machine's organization but differs because life and motion originate from within; identity depends on continued organization and common life, not strict sameness of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A watch analogy: machine organization without internal life vs. animals where internal motion and life co-begin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of man depends on the same continued life
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of a man consists in participation of the same continued life communicated to successive particles of matter united to the organized body; identity is not merely unity of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues this avoids absurd conclusions (e.g., that widely spaced historical persons could be the same if only 'soul' identity were asserted without bodily continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of identity must suit the idea to which it is applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity criteria vary with the name/idea (substance, man, person); to judge identity rightly one must attend to what the name stands for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusions arise when 'person', 'man', and 'substance' are used interchangeably despite denoting different ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity defined as sameness of a thinking, self-conscious being
rubrics_metrics.description: A PERSON is a thinking, intelligent being that has reason and reflection and can consider itself as the same thinking thing in different times and places by consciousness; personal identity consists in this self-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As far as consciousness (the ability to repeat past perceptions with the same awareness) extends backward, so far personal identity extends; memory/consciousness continuity grounds personal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is inseparable from thinking and grounds the self
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness always accompanies thinking and makes every one to himself that which he calls self; it is impossible to perceive without perceiving that one perceives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes present sensations and perceptions as the basis of self; interruption of consciousness (forgetfulness, sleep) raises philosophical puzzles but not about personal identity itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity distinct from identity of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity concerns what makes the same person (consciousness), not whether the same identical substance persists; consciousness may persist even if substances change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different substances could be united into one person by the same consciousness, analogous to how different material particles can compose the same living animal by a continued life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity can persist through change of bodily substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of the body may be separated (cut off) and cease to be part of the self because they lose their connection to consciousness, yet personal identity can remain as the substance composing the person varies while consciousness persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a hand cut off is no longer part of that which is himself; this shows bodily substance may change without losing personal identity so long as consciousness remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of personal identity across change of thinking substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the same thinking substance changed can still be the same person cannot be resolved without knowing the nature of thinking substances and whether consciousness can transfer between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same consciousness could be continued or transferred, it would determine personal identity; Locke leaves this to metaphysical inquiry about the nature of thinking substances.
